title: quantized-path-throughput-probing-playbook
body:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for probing throughput on quantized execution paths (int8 / fp16 variants) in the serving runtime. Goal: get repeatable, comparable throughput numbers between unquantized and quantized variants while accounting for the extra sources of variance that quantization introduces (kernel switching, memory layout, micro-batching differences).

Scope / when to use:
- Use when validating a candidate quantization profile before promoting it to a canary rollout.
- Intended for hardware families: A100(80GB), H100, and an x86 CPU baseline for small models.
- Not for latency SLO microbenchmarks (separate tail-latency playbook exists) — this focuses on sustained throughput and repeatability.

Quick summary of the approach (one-liner):
Stabilize thermal and kernel caches -> deterministic synthetic load profile (mixed sequence lengths) -> long ramp-to-plateau with pinned RNG seeds -> capture windows after steady-state confirmed -> compare per-token cost and occupancy between quantized and baseline.

Testbed and hardware hygiene:
- Machines should be fully isolated: single test VM per GPU card where possible, NVIDIA persistence mode on, power profile fixed to "prefer maximum performance".
- Cool-down period: ensure nodes start at <40C GPU die temp when beginning runs. If not, include a 20-minute idle cool-down.
- Set CPU governor to performance. Disable background cloud agents and cron jobs on test hosts.
- Ensure same CUDA / cuDNN / kernel versions across compared runs. Record driver versions in run metadata.

Load generator config (recommended template):
- Client concurrency model: 32 worker processes, each with an async event loop. Use tokenized request payloads (standardized prompt templates).
- Arrival pattern: Poisson with mean inter-arrival varied per sweep; for ramps use a linear 15-minute ramp to target qps.
- Sequence length distribution: use 70/20/10 split for short(16), medium(128), long(512) tokens to approximate production mix for conversational endpoints.
- Batching policy: allow runtime batching up to 256 tokens per batch; record effective batch sizes.
- Warmstart flag: run a separate priming pass with 10% of target QPS for 5 minutes before starting ramp; see warmup section.

Quantized-specific knobs to capture in metadata:
- Quantization profile id (QA-tag), lowering backend (x86-vector / triton-kernel / custom-kernel), calibration method used (min/max or percentile 99.9), per-layer fallback list.
- Whether KV cache uses quantized cache (if supported) or uses fp16 fallback.

Warmup and repeatability strategy:
- Rationale: quantized kernels can cause transient slowdowns during first N invocations because of dynamic kernel selection, GPU memory re-layout, and JIT/dispatch caches. Without a deterministic warmup we will observe non-repeatable throughput and phantom regressions.
- Two-phase warmup: (1) Kernel-stabilize: 5–10 full-size inference requests (long tokens) with pinned RNG to populate kernels and allocate large buffers; (2) Occupancy-stabilize: run a 10-minute walk-up where qps steps from 10% to 50% of target to exercise batching heuristics.
- After warmup, wait a 2-minute idle settle period to allow telemetry to flush, then start the ramp-to-plateau sweep.
- For seed hygiene, use the same pseudo-random sequence of prompts across compared runs. Store the seed and the prompt corpus version in metadata.

Repeatability checklist (pre-run):
- [ ] Node rebooted or state-cleared since previous run (note: reboot reduces thermal drift variation).
- [ ] Driver/runtime versions recorded.
- [ ] Power profile and CPU governor set.
- [ ] Prompts corpus SHA, RNG seed, and client binary SHA in metadata.
- [ ] Quantization profile and fallback list recorded.
- [ ] Background noise check: ping and cpu_util traces show low background activity.

Run schedule and measurement windows:
- Run length: each sweep target should run for 30 minutes after ramp-to-plateau confirmation (see plateau detection).
- Ramp: linear 15-minute ramp to target qps (use 1-min step granularity).
- Plateau detection: require 10-minute contiguous window where GPU occupancy and per-second throughput variance < 2% to declare steady-state. If plateau not observed, extend run by 15 minutes and re-evaluate.
- Capture windows: discard first 20% of steady-state window for transient guard, then use next 10-minute block as canonical measurement.

Metrics to collect (minimum):
- Per-request: total latency (p50/p90/p99), token-level latency, response size, model version, quant flag.
- Per-second: throughput (requests/sec and tokens/sec), effective batch size distribution, GPU SM utilization, GPU memory used, DMA stalls, kernel uptime counts (if available).
- Environmental: GPU die temp, power draw, CPU util, network egress, system interrupts.
- Runtime-specific: cache hit rate (prefix/KV), kernel-switch counts, per-layer quantization fallback counter.

Analysis steps and delta checks:
- Normalize throughput to tokens/sec to make fair comparisons across sequence-distribution differences.
- Compute per-token latency and per-token compute cost: tokens/sec per GPU and tokens/sec per active SM.
- Identify difference windows: align timestamps and compute 1-minute rolling ratio of quantized/baseline throughput. Highlight sustained deviations >3%.
- Correlate any dips with kernel-switch events, cache miss spikes, or thermal rise.

Common failure modes we've observed:
- 1) Initial kernel dispatch overhead: short-lived but can ruin short runs. Fix: longer warmup and longer measurement windows.
- 2) Memory layout churn: quantized kernels sometimes re-allocate large buffers N+1 times; visible as repeated GC-like memory churn. Fix: ensure priming uses long sequences and pinned allocation paths are exercised.
- 3) Micro-batching oscillation: batching heuristics flip between batch sizes under certain arrival jitters producing throughput oscillation. Fix: use stabilized arrival (Poisson) and capture batch-size distributions.

Diagnostics artifacts to collect on failure:
- Full kernel dispatch logs (runtime debug level), per-layer profiler traces, nvml logs (sm utilization, temp), client-side request logs (with seeds), and a flamegraph of runtime CPU threads for the measurement period.

Example commands / snippets (conceptual):
- Start client with seed and corpus: ./loadbench --corpus=corpus-v12.json --seed=42 --arrival=poisson --target-qps=1200 --ramp-mins=15 --clients=32 --emit-metrics=/tmp/run123.metrics
- Server: ENABLE_QUANTIZED_PATH=1 ./serve --model=my-model@v3 --profiling=kernel-dispatch:debug --export-kernel-stats=/tmp/ks.json

Reporting and pass/fail criteria:
- Pass: quantized path tokens/sec >= baseline tokens/sec * (1 - 0.05) AND p99 latency <= baseline p99 * 1.1 AND no sustained (>2 minutes) kernel fallback events.
- Soft-fail (requires investigation): tokens/sec regressions between 5% and 15% or intermittent kernel fallbacks with <1% frequency.
- Hard fail: >15% sustained throughput regression OR repeated memory churn events causing retries or OOMs.

Suggested dashboard panels and alert rules for benchmarking runs:
- Tokens/sec (5s, 1m), effective batch size histogram, kernel-fallback-rate (1m), GPU temp & power, rolling throughput ratio (quantized/baseline) with red threshold at 0.85.

Post-run artifact checklist:
- [ ] Attach NVML CSV, kernel-stats JSON, client metrics JSON, run metadata JSON.
- [ ] Upload flamegraph and per-layer traces to the run folder on S3.
- [ ] Create a short summary in the benchmarking Confluence page with key deltas and whether to proceed to canary.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we standardize on a single mixed-length distribution globally? (pros: comparability, cons: not match customer tail cases)
- Add automated detection to pause run if kernel-fallback spikes >0.5% in a minute.
- Evaluate effect of using deterministic batching (force batch sizes) vs letting runtime heuristics govern for production realism.

Notes / history:
- Inspired by a few runs where quantized rollout produced sporadic 10-40% regressions on H100 under long-sequence synthetic traffic (see ENG-1289).
- Prior experiments showed thermal stabilization reduced variance by ~3–5 percentage points on identical workloads.

Contact for questions: Priya Desai (eng-serving-runtime).

This is a working doc — keep updates here rather than creating forks.
